I have mine set at the coldest setting, which does hit the "high 30s" claim at 38 degrees Fahrenheit. It would be nice if it could get a bit colder, but it gets the job done. It will take a while for a full fridge to cool, so you're better off loading it half way and then adding more cans rather than adding a bunch of warm cans at once.

You can make it work - The description says it can be expanded to 29.5 inches (75cm) but if you do that, the aluminum bars holding it to the corners will have less than 1 inch of the bar inside of each end. This is not enough to hold 440 lbs. I would say that 30 lbs at full extension is about all it will hold up. The only way it will hold 440 lbs is when the unit is fully collapsed and that size was too small for my refrigerator. The aluminum bars are 1-inch square bars that slide into the corner piece made of heavy-duty plastic and that snug connection gives the stand its strength. The aluminum bars are very very thin and upgrading the quality of the bars will give a lot of strength to the stand. As-is, this unit would not hold the Galanz refrigerator I have pictured.

I did modify the stand. First I threw away the cheap aluminum bars. I could bend them with my bare hands without much difficulty. Next, I went to a big box home improvement store and purchased a 1-inch square steel bar (which cost more than the stand). After cutting the steel bar to length and tapping them into the corner pieces, the strength became a lot more than 440 lbs.

Bottom line is that as described, the sturdiness of the stand reduces significantly as you expand the stand length and width. The specs must describe the stand when it's fully collapsed. With a little know-how, you can make this work better by upgrading the length and strength of the bars.

Rusty ice maker - The ice maker makes rusty ice. The metal that should be stainless steel or rust resistant, is rusty and leaves you with rusty ice cubes or rusty crushed ice. If you put your ice in dark drink (tea, coke, beer, etc) you would never know. But plop some ice in milk or empty glass wrapped in a paper towel, and you'll notice small orangish brown spots on the ice. Inspect the ice maker to find rusty parts. I called Frigidair and they said they have a "specific clause in their warranty that say's they do not cover rusty parts". To put such a clause makes it seem evident that it was a planned problem in production from the beginning. It will take about 8-12months for you to start to see rust. Most people never notice or check. Even though none of their employees would like to be served a glass of rusty ice.
